narrative.what_i_did:
The operator opened with /clear and 'Continue where they left you.' I grounded against the prior session.json — the previous carpenter shipped the tree-v2 family ring and left field-testing on a real phone as the honest next move, but field-testing happens on the operator's iPhone not in this sandbox, so the carpenter side was at a clean break and the next cut needed direction. The chip-form chooser I surfaced offered the four threads the handoff named — WalletProvider extraction with its structural 797-of-800 deadline as the Recommended pick, tap-for-detail on family-ring nodes, the operator's own add-birthday-now backdated credential, or pausing the carpenter to let the operator field-test first. The operator picked WalletProvider extraction.

Before touching code I read the whole 797-line WalletProvider top to bottom to ground against what the prior carpenter had named. Then I asked a sub-chip-form: useChatTransport (biggest headroom — lifts the whole chat-thread concern as one cohesive unit, ~150 lines), usePeerOps (lowest risk — pulls four small callbacks, ~60 lines), or useInboxSubscription (most invasive — splits the Mycelium effect itself). The operator picked useChatTransport. I read the Subscription and Transport contracts to confirm close() is idempotent on both before committing to the cleanest lifecycle pattern, then read useChatPersistence to confirm its signature stayed importable into the new hook.

I cut a new file at src/features/messaging/useChatTransport.ts that owns the per-peer chat substrate as one cohesive unit. The hook takes transport, wallet, ownerId, and passphrase as inputs and exposes chatThreadsByPeer, sendChatMessage, and purgePeerThread. Inside it owns the chatThreadsByPeer state, the chatSubRef, the chat-kind subscription effect bound to (transport, wallet), the full sendChatMessage callback including the optimistic-append plus publish-result reconciliation plus the fail-path optimistic-record purge plus the pending-path warning surface, the purgePeerThread helper for removePeerConnection, and the useChatPersistence wiring. The whole concern that was scattered across WalletProvider — state declaration, subscription nested inside the inbox effect, ninety-eight-line sendChatMessage callback, peer-thread purge inlined in removePeerConnection, persistence call near the bottom — now lives as one consumable unit at a single import site.

The WalletProvider edits ran in five passes. First I dropped the now-unused imports — summarizePublish, InboxChatMessage, ThreadMessage, useChatPersistence — and added the useChatTransport import. Second I replaced transportRef with const transport state and removed both chatThreadsByPeer state and chatSubRef so the inbox effect could lift transport availability into React state where the chat hook can react to it. Third I stripped the nested chat-subscribe block out of the inbox effect and changed transportRef.current writes into setTransport calls; the inbox effect still owns transport open and close lifecycle, the chat hook just rides on the state. Fourth I updated sendEnvelope and syncEnvelope to read transport from the state closure rather than the ref — both callbacks now include transport in their dep arrays and regenerate on transport changes. Fifth I added the useChatTransport hook call right before removePeerConnection so purgePeerThread was in scope, replaced the inline chat-thread purge inside removePeerConnection with a single purgePeerThread call, and removed the standalone useChatPersistence line that the hook now wires internally.

Final state: one new file at 221 lines, WalletProvider down to 653 lines from 797 — a 144-line reduction giving 147 lines of headroom under the 800 hard limit, more than enough runway for the next forced extraction. The messaging manifest gained useChatTransport.ts in touches and the notes paragraph explains the 2026-05-27 extraction's structural role plus the transport-state lift. All four gates green throughout — typecheck silent, lint silent, 335 of 335 tests passing in 9.95s with the file-size doctrine now warning at 654 instead of 797 for WalletProvider, build clean with the HomeScreen bundle unchanged at 22.17KB gz under the 22.5KB budget.

narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
Two honest observations. First, the transport-state lift I made changes the reference-identity of sendEnvelope and syncEnvelope on transport open and close events. Previously those callbacks were stable across the whole unlocked-phase lifetime because they only depended on phase and read transport from a ref. Now they regenerate whenever transport state changes. The WalletContextValue memo accordingly regenerates on those changes, and every consumer that destructures sendEnvelope or syncEnvelope from useWallet gets a fresh reference. In practice transport changes are rare events tied to opt-in, opt-out, lock, unlock, and Wallet.rotate — at most a few times per session — so the re-render storm is bounded. But a consumer that uses sendEnvelope inside its own useCallback dep array would see that callback regenerate too, cascading. None surfaced in the test run but it is worth flagging if a future session notices unexpected re-renders in components that hold sendEnvelope or syncEnvelope.

Second, I considered keeping transportRef alongside the new transport state for source-of-truth purity and rejected it. The ref-plus-state duality would have preserved sendEnvelope and syncEnvelope's reference stability with the cost of two state-and-ref pairs needing to be kept in lockstep on every open and close. The cleaner-source-of-truth path I took has the rerender consequence above; the dual-source path would have avoided that at the cost of two-source-of-truth confusion. The choice was deliberate but reasonable people could land on the other answer. If field-testing surfaces a rerender problem we have an easy revert path.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching this session is what a clean hook extraction earns over the long run of a provider growing past its size budget. WalletProvider had become a kitchen-sink — passphrase prompt phase, onboarding bundle consumption, anchor worker, transport open and close, inbox envelope subscription, chat-kind subscription, sendEnvelope, syncEnvelope, sendChatMessage, anchor confirmation back-attachment, identity ceremony coupling, save, refresh, updatePrefs, unhold, removePeerConnection, idle lock, theme paint, chat persistence, and the context value memo all in one file. The 800-line hard limit is the codebase's enforcement that no single file should carry that many concerns. The extraction this session did not just move lines out — it moved a whole concern out, the per-peer chat substrate, and the concern's boundaries are now visible. The hook has explicit inputs (transport, wallet, ownerId, passphrase) and explicit outputs (chatThreadsByPeer, sendChatMessage, purgePeerThread). Future modifications to chat behavior land in one file. Future modifications to provider behavior do not have to reason about chat at all.

The second teaching is what 'lifting transport from ref to state' unlocks. The ref pattern is a common one for values that need to be reached from multiple callbacks but should not trigger re-renders. The ref worked perfectly for sendEnvelope and syncEnvelope and the old nested chat subscription because they all lived inside the same provider. The moment one of them moves to a sibling hook, the ref stops working — refs do not propagate across hook boundaries because hooks at the same level cannot read each other's refs. State propagates through arguments. The lift was structurally required for the extraction, not optional. The cost is reference-identity churn on the callbacks that read transport, the benefit is the chat hook can subscribe and tear down purely from its own effect lifecycle without WalletProvider needing to call into it on transport changes. This is the React-idiomatic shape: lift state up to where multiple hooks need to read it, pass it down as props or arguments.

The broader thesis-level connection is that WalletProvider is the wallet's runtime brain — it holds keys, session, phase, holdings, transport, and orchestrates the lifecycle of every operation that touches them. Every line in that file is in some sense load-bearing for the operator's sovereign-identity story. Letting it grow without extraction would have eventually meant the operator's wallet had a 1500-line monolith at its core, and changes to messaging would risk breaking onboarding, changes to anchoring would risk breaking transport, changes to one phase transition would risk leaking into another. Pulling concerns out into named hooks with explicit inputs and outputs is what keeps the wallet's brain inspectable as it grows. The chat substrate left first because the operator picked it; the next forced extraction will follow the same pattern; eventually WalletProvider becomes a thin orchestrator of well-named hooks rather than the place every wallet operation accidentally ends up. That is the architectural arc this cut is one stop along.

feedback_to_appcommander: The two-stage chip-form pattern landed cleanly this session. First chip-form chose the thread (WalletProvider extraction), second chip-form within the same task chose the substructure (which hook to extract). The operator did not have to choose between three hook names without context — the descriptions on each chip-form option named the line counts, the blast radii, and the trade-offs. The PFOR-019 doctrine reading is that nested chip-forms for sub-decisions inside a chosen thread is the right pattern when the carpenter has the information needed to bound the choice but the operator owns the architectural preference. One suggestion: consider naming this two-stage pattern explicitly in the skeleton doctrine so future carpenters reach for it without having to discover it from precedent.
